topic: Internet Stories ep.6: Hotmail's email footer. Launched July 4 1996 as free web-browser email (email was usually tied to your internet provider); founders wanted billboards, investor (Tim Draper, unnamed in reel) said too expensive and pushed a line at the bottom of every email ('PS: I love you. Get your free email at Hotmail'); founders hated it, cut 'I love you', kept the link; every email became a free ad from a friend; 9M+ users by end of 1997 (Microsoft release); Microsoft bought it Dec 1997, reportedly ~$400M (terms undisclosed). Lesson: everything you send is marketing, put your website link on email signature, invoices, quotes.
hook: One email footer turned a tiny startup into a $400 million company.

topic: Internet Stories ep.7: the Oct 4 2021 Facebook outage. A command during routine maintenance (meant to check backbone capacity) cut every link between Facebook's data centres; its DNS servers withdrew their routes so the 'internet's phone book' had no answer and Facebook/Instagram/WhatsApp didn't exist to phones; staff reportedly couldn't get into buildings with badges (NYT via Wikipedia); engineers went to the data centres in person; ~6 hours. Lesson: social media is rented land, your website is land you own.

topic: Website tip: stop using a PDF menu. On a phone it downloads, opens tiny (pinch/zoom/scroll sideways), is often out of date because one price change means a new file, and a scanned-photo menu can't be read by screen readers (BOIA). Fix: menu as a normal web page with real text, prices, GF/vegan tags; quick price edits; keep a small printable PDF link at the bottom. Made-up business Pebble Lane Kitchen.

Internet Stories ep.8: the first web banner ad. AT&T on HotWired (Wired magazine's website), October 1994: 'Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? You will.' About 44% clicked (agency's recalled figure). HotWired sold page space like a magazine to pay writers; a spot reportedly cost $30,000 for 3 months. It led to a page of art museum sites, not a sales pitch. Today banner ads get clicked by well under 1 in 100; banner blindness means flashy boxes get skipped, so keep key website info clear and plain.

topic: Website tip: ugly link previews. When you send your website link the preview shows no picture, a title of 'Home' and random footer text. Previews come from Open Graph tags (og:title, og:description, og:image) that Messages, WhatsApp and Facebook read; missing tags = app guesses. Fix: share image ~1200x630, title = what you do + where, one line on why pick you; Wix/Squarespace/Shopify have a social share image setting; send the link to yourself to check. Made-up business Ridgeway Roofing, Toowoomba.

topic: Internet Stories ep.9: Gap's 2010 logo change. New logo (plain black letters, small blue square) quietly appeared on gap.com in Oct 2010; 1,000+ negative Facebook comments, a parody Twitter account; Gap asked customers for design ideas (crowdsourcing), which made it worse; about a week later Gap went back to the blue box (Gap North America president Marka Hansen: 'we did not go about this in the right way'). Lesson: people recognise logos rather than read them; keep what's familiar and test redesigns with real customers.

topic: Internet Stories ep.10: the Trojan Room coffee pot. Cambridge University Computer Lab, 1991: staff climbed several flights of stairs to find the shared pot empty, so two researchers (Quentin Stafford-Fraser, Paul Jardetzky; unnamed in reel) pointed a camera at it and wrote XCoffee in about a day; tiny greyscale image updated ~3x a minute; on the World Wide Web Nov 1993; hundreds of thousands looked at it; switched off Aug 2001 when the lab moved; one of the pots sold on eBay for £3,350 (to Spiegel Online). Lesson: your website should answer 'is it worth the trip?' (hours, prices, stock). Made-up business Fernhill Hardware, Katoomba.

topic: Website tip: business email on @gmail.com vs your own domain. Anyone can make a free Gmail with your business name in minutes, so customers can't tell a real quote from a scammer's look-alike; jess@yourbusiness.com.au matches your website and only the domain owner can create addresses on it; Google Workspace / Microsoft 365 let you use your own domain inside Gmail or Outlook; ask your setup person to turn on email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) so quotes don't land in spam. Made-up business Kestrel Plumbing, Geelong. Light warm-white reel style.

Internet Stories ep.11: the first spam email. 3 May 1978, a DEC marketer (Gary Thuerk, unnamed in reel) emailed an invite to DECSYSTEM-20 open houses (Los Angeles, San Mateo) to hundreds of ARPANET users on the West Coast at once (ARPANET = US government network linking universities and labs, a few thousand users, email for work, no ads); furious replies, one said it shut down his system; ARPANET administrators reprimanded him; he later claimed it paid off. Named 'spam' after the Monty Python sketch (early 1990s). Lesson: email works only to people who said yes; Australia's Spam Act: consent, identify yourself, working unsubscribe.

topic: Website tip: who actually owns your website? If your web designer disappeared, could you still change it? Often the designer bought the domain, set up hosting and kept every login, so you pay for a site you don't control. Own 3 things in your name: the domain (registered to your business, your own login; if it's in someone else's account and a renewal is missed, site and email can stop working), hosting (your own account or at least admin access), logins (website admin, Google Business Profile, analytics). Asking isn't rude. Made-up business Wattlebank Landscaping, Toowoomba.
